slides.title: How long until your money doubles?
slides.sub: One mental math trick: the Rule of 72

slides.heading: The rule
slides.big: 72 ÷ your yearly return = years to double
body: Divide 72 by the yearly return you expect. The answer is roughly how many years it takes your money to double.

slides.heading: Try it
slides.note: Higher returns usually come with more risk.

slides.heading: Why starting early wins
slides.intro: One $1,000 deposit growing at 9% a year:

slides.takeaway: Time does the heavy lifting. Start small, but start now.

posts.caption:
Quick math trick: divide 72 by your yearly return to see how many years it takes your money to double.

At 9%, that's about 8 years. Start at 18 and a single $1,000 could grow to around $16,000 by age 50 without adding another dollar. Returns aren't guaranteed, but time is the biggest advantage you have right now.

slides.title: Why is my paycheck smaller than I expected?
slides.sub: Gross pay vs. net pay, explained

slides.heading: Two numbers on every paycheck
items: What you earned before anything comes out
What actually lands in your account

slides.heading: Where the difference goes
slides.note: Federal income tax depends on how much you earn and your W-4. Texas has no state income tax.

slides.heading: Example: $500 gross pay
slides.note: Part-time workers often get some or all of their federal income tax back when they file a tax return.

slides.takeaway: Budget with your net pay, not your gross pay. And file a tax return. You might get money back.

posts.caption:
Got your first paycheck and it's less than you thought? That's the difference between gross pay and net pay.

Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%) come out of every check, plus federal income tax based on your pay and your W-4. Good news if you work in Texas: there's no state income tax.

If you work part-time, file a tax return. You might get some of that federal tax back.

slides.title: What actually moves your credit score?
slides.sub: The 5 factors behind your FICO score

slides.heading: Focus on the big two
body: Payment history and amounts owed make up most of your score.
Pay every bill on time, every time. Keep your balance low compared to your limit.

slides.heading: Example: $1,000 credit limit
slides.note: Lower usage generally helps. A common rule of thumb is to stay under 30%.

slides.takeaway: Pay on time, keep balances low, and give your credit time to grow.

posts.caption:
Your credit score isn't a mystery. FICO scores come down to 5 factors, and two of them (payment history and amounts owed) make up 65% of the score.

Pay on time, every time. Keep your balance low compared to your limit. On a $1,000 limit, carrying $100 looks a lot better than carrying $300.

slides.title: The simplest budget that actually works

slides.heading: Split your take-home pay 3 ways
items: Emergency fund, investing, paying off debt

slides.heading: Example: $800 a month
slides.note: Living at home with fewer bills? Shift some of your needs money into savings while you can.

slides.heading: $160 a month adds up
body: That's saved before earning a single dollar of interest.

slides.takeaway: Pay yourself first. Move your savings the day you get paid.

posts.caption:
Budgeting doesn't have to be complicated. Try the 50/30/20 rule: 50% of your take-home pay for needs, 30% for wants, 20% for savings.

On $800 a month, that's $160 saved. Do that for a year and you've got $1,920 before any interest. Still living at home? Push that savings number even higher while your bills are low.

slides.sub: Why so many investors start here

slides.heading: What is an index fund?
slides.big: One fund, a whole slice of the market
body: An S&P 500 index fund owns shares of about 500 of the largest US companies, all in one purchase.

slides.heading: Why people like them
items: Hundreds of companies in one buy
Nobody is paid to pick stocks

slides.heading: Fees matter more than you think
slides.intro: $10,000 for 30 years, assuming a 7% yearly return before fees:
slides.note: Same investment. The fee costs you about $18,000.

slides.takeaway: Broad and low cost beats complicated. Always check the expense ratio.

posts.caption:
An index fund lets you own a slice of the whole market in one purchase. An S&P 500 index fund holds about 500 of the biggest US companies.

The part most people miss: fees. $10,000 growing for 30 years at 7% before fees ends up around $75,500 with a 0.03% fee, but only about $57,400 with a 1% fee. That's roughly $18,000 lost to fees.
